Neutron. An uncharged subatomic particle found in atomic nuclei, except in hydrogen-1, composed of three quarks and roughly equal in mass to protons. Slightly heavier than protons and unstable when free with a half-life of about ten minutes, neutrons stabilize nuclei against electromagnetic repulsion and are essential for all complex atoms. Their discovery in 1932 by James Chadwick completed the model of atomic structure and unlocked nuclear chemistry and physics.

An uncharged baryon composed of one up quark and two down quarks, the neutron has a mass of approximately 1.675 times ten to the negative twenty-seventh kilograms, slightly heavier than a proton by about 1.8 megaelectron volts per speed-of-light squared. Stable inside nuclei, it decays when free via beta-minus decay, where the neutron becomes a proton, an electron, and an antineutrino, with a half-life of roughly 886 seconds, or about fifteen minutes.

The number of neutrons determines isotope identity. Varying the number of neutrons for a fixed proton number creates stable or radioactive isotopes. For light elements, stable nuclei have roughly equal numbers of protons and neutrons. Heavier nuclei require excess neutrons for stability. Nuclear stability depends on the balance of the strong nuclear force, which is attractive and short-range, versus electromagnetic repulsion, which is repulsive and long-range.

Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932 through beryllium bombardment by alpha particles, completing the model of atomic structure. Critical in nuclear fission, one neutron strikes a fissile nucleus like uranium-235, producing two to three secondary neutrons that trigger a chain reaction. Slow neutrons, or thermals, are more likely to induce fission in uranium-235, while fast neutrons preferentially cause uranium-238 capture without fission. Used in neutron activation analysis to detect trace elements, neutron scattering probes material structure with wavelengths matching atomic spacings.

Neutron stars are collapsed stellar cores supported by neutron degeneracy pressure, extremely dense—a teaspoon of neutron-star material weighs about six billion tons. Thermal neutrons are essential for nuclear reactor operation. They sustain chain reactions in fissile materials like uranium.
